data.title: Acanthosis nigricans — viva
data.summary: Pigmentary disorders · 16 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Acanthosis nigricans** (Pigmentary disorders)_

**Q1. Define acanthosis nigricans (AN).**
- Symmetrical, velvety, hyperpigmented thickening of skin, especially in flexures (neck, axillae, groin, antecubital, submammary, umbilicus, knuckles); a cutaneous marker of insulin resistance or, rarely, internal malignancy

**Q2. Classify AN (Curth/Schwartz).**
- Benign hereditary (autosomal dominant; FGFR3 — childhood onset)
- Obesity-associated (pseudoacanthosis nigricans — commonest)
- Syndromic: insulin resistance syndromes — type A (insulin receptor mutation, HAIR-AN: Hyperandrogenism, Insulin Resistance, AN), type B (anti-insulin receptor antibodies — autoimmune), lipodystrophies, Rabson–Mendenhall, Donohue (leprechaunism), PCOS, Crouzon/FGFR3 syndromes (SADDAN)
- Malignant AN: sudden, extensive, rapidly progressive, with mucosal and palmar involvement — gastric adenocarcinoma (commonest), other GI, lung, ovary
- Drug-induced: systemic corticosteroids, nicotinic acid, insulin injections (local), OCP, protease inhibitors, testosterone
- Acral (acral acanthotic anomaly — dorsa of hands/feet, darker skin), unilateral (naevoid), mixed

**Q3. Explain the pathogenesis.**
- Hyperinsulinaemia → insulin binds IGF-1 receptors on keratinocytes and fibroblasts → proliferation
- Malignant AN: tumour-derived growth factors — TGF-α (EGFR activation), IGF-1, FGF
- Genetic: activating FGFR3 mutations (keratinocyte FGFR signalling)
- Friction and moisture in flexures contribute

**Q4. Clinical features.**
- Grey-brown velvety plaques with accentuated skin markings; later verrucous/papillomatous; skin tags (acrochordons) common in the same areas; mild itch
- Severity graded by Burke's scale (neck 0–4; texture 0–3)
- Malignant AN: older, non-obese, rapid onset, extensive (including unusual sites), oral mucosa (papillomatosis of lips/tongue), palms (tripe palms — rugose velvety thickening of palms), Leser–Trélat sign (eruptive seborrhoeic keratoses), florid cutaneous papillomatosis, weight loss

**Q5. What are tripe palms and the sign of Leser–Trélat?**
- Tripe palms: acquired velvety, thickened palms with pronounced dermatoglyphics — paraneoplastic (lung cancer when isolated; gastric when with AN)
- Leser–Trélat: sudden eruption/increase in size and number of seborrhoeic keratoses — paraneoplastic (GI adenocarcinoma, lymphoma)

**Q6. Histopathology.**
- Papillomatosis and hyperkeratosis (finger-like upward projections of dermal papillae) with mild acanthosis and minimal hyperpigmentation — the brown colour is mostly from hyperkeratosis, not melanin

**Q7. Differential diagnosis.**
- Confluent and reticulated papillomatosis (trunk; responds to minocycline), Dowling–Degos disease (reticulate flexural pigmentation, comedo-like pits), terra firma-forme dermatosis (dirt — wipes off with alcohol), erythrasma, pellagra (Casal's), Addison's, haemochromatosis, LPP inverse type, seborrhoeic keratosis, epidermal naevus, frictional melanosis

**Q8. Investigations.**
- BMI, waist circumference, BP; fasting glucose, HbA1c, fasting insulin (HOMA-IR), lipid profile, liver enzymes (NAFLD)
- Women: menstrual history, hirsutism — testosterone, DHEAS, LH/FSH, pelvic ultrasound (PCOS)
- Malignant AN suspicion: CBC, upper GI endoscopy, CT abdomen/chest, tumour markers
- Thyroid, cortisol (Cushing's) if indicated

**Q9. Treatment.**
- Treat cause: weight loss, exercise, dietary change, metformin (improves insulin resistance), pioglitazone; PCOS management (OCP, spironolactone); stop offending drug; treat malignancy (AN regresses with tumour removal)
- Topical: retinoids (tretinoin 0.05–0.1%, adapalene), keratolytics (salicylic acid, urea, lactic/glycolic acid), vitamin D analogues (calcipotriol), trichloroacetic acid peels, topical metformin
- Systemic: oral retinoids (isotretinoin/acitretin), omega-3 fatty acids, octreotide (selected)
- Procedures: long-pulsed alexandrite/Q-switched/fractional CO2 lasers, dermabrasion; remove skin tags

**Q10. Why is AN important?**
- Easily visible marker of insulin resistance, metabolic syndrome, prediabetes/type 2 diabetes, PCOS and NAFLD — screening opportunity in children and adolescents; rarely heralds internal malignancy

**Q11. Dermoscopy findings.**
- Brown-grey 'crista cutis' (elevated ridges) and 'sulcus cutis' (furrows) pattern, papillomatous projections, hyperpigmented dots, no vessels — distinguishes from DDD and CARP

**Q12. What is the Burke scale?**
- Neck severity 0–4 (0 absent, 1 visible on close inspection, 2 limited to base of skull, 3 extending laterally, 4 visible anteriorly) + texture 0–3 (smooth to extremely coarse/ raised); also grades axilla, knuckles, elbows, knees — correlates with insulin levels

**Q13. Describe HAIR-AN syndrome.**
- Hyperandrogenism (hirsutism, acne, irregular menses), Insulin Resistance, Acanthosis Nigricans — adolescent girls, variant of PCOS; treat with weight loss, metformin, OCPs/ spironolactone

**Q14. What is the association with obesity in Indian children?**
- Indian children have higher insulin resistance at lower BMI ('thin-fat' phenotype); AN in a child is a marker for prediabetes/ type 2 diabetes — check fasting glucose, insulin, HbA1c, lipids, BP

**Q15. Treatment response expectations.**
- AN improves slowly over months with weight loss and insulin sensitisers; topical therapy gives cosmetic improvement; recurrence if weight regained; malignant AN improves after cancer treatment and reappears with recurrence

**Q16. How does Wood's lamp help in pigmentary disorders?**
- 365 nm UVA absorbed by epidermal melanin: epidermal hyperpigmentation is accentuated (melasma epidermal type, freckles, CALM), dermal pigment is not; depigmentation (vitiligo, piebaldism) shows bright chalk-white; hypopigmentation (nevus depigmentosus, PA, IGH) shows dull off-white; also fluorescence of infections (PV yellow, erythrasma coral-red)

## Quick spotter facts
- Velvety dark neck/axillae in an obese adolescent — AN (insulin resistance)
- Sudden extensive AN + tripe palms + Leser–Trélat — gastric cancer
- HAIR-AN syndrome

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Acanthosis nigricans). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
